I believe governments should legally recognize same-sex marriage nationwide.

My reasoning rests on several foundations. First, there's a straightforward fairness principle: if marriage licenses convey legal benefits—tax treatment, hospital visitation rights, inheritance protections—denying them based on sexual orientation creates arbitrary discrimination. The characteristics that make someone a good spouse (commitment, care, stability) have nothing to do with whether they're attracted to the same or opposite sex.

Second, religious objections to same-sex relationships, while sincere for many, don't justify legal exclusion in diverse societies. People can maintain their own religious beliefs while the state provides equal civil protections. Many religious communities support same-sex marriage anyway.

Third, empirical evidence matters: decades of experience in countries and regions with legal same-sex marriage shows no harmful effects on heterosexual marriages, children, or social stability. The predicted harms haven't materialized.

I recognize this involves real value disagreements about sexuality and tradition. But the burden of proof should rest on those proposing legal restrictions—and the case for restricting others' civil rights based on contested moral claims seems weak.

The practical alternative—a patchwork of state-by-state rules—creates unnecessary confusion and denies equal protection. Nationwide recognition respects both the dignity of same-sex couples and the religious freedom of those who disagree with same-sex relationships personally.
